The player hums into the wider, flatter side; the oscillating air pressure of the humming sets the membrane vibrating, and pitch and volume follow the humming. A beginner can first practise humming a steady single pitch, then use syllables such as “doo”, “too” and “hoo” and a trill, and notice how different articulation changes the timbre. The basic point is a steady, clear voice, not how hard you blow.

Classical works are rare; David Bedford's 《100 Kazoos》, the rondo of the first hymn of Leonard Bernstein's 《Mass》 and Charles Ives's 《Yale-Princeton Football Game》 use kazoo ensembles. Its range is relatively limited, mostly the upper-middle register, and the volume is moderate but penetrating. Through the resonance and amplification of the internal membrane, the instrument turns the subtle vibration of the voice into a special nasal quality, producing a sound like a saxophone but rougher and funnier. Compared with the bright harmonica the kazoo is heavier; compared with the round saxophone it is a little frayed. This timbre has made it widely used in jazz, folk and pop music, adding fun and familiarity.

The kazoo is a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 242, in the mirliton class: a vibrating membrane alters the player's voice to produce a buzzing timbre. The player does not blow but hums into the wider, flatter side, and the oscillating air pressure sets the membrane vibrating, so pitch and volume follow the humming, and syllables such as “doo” and “too” also change the timbre. It is one of the non-electronic instruments developed in the United States; professional players use it in jug bands and comedy music, and amateurs use it widely; it also appears in youth jazz bands in north-east England and south Wales, at the Cádiz carnival in Spain and in Uruguayan murga processions.

靠人聲哼唱的簡易膜鳴樂器至少自16世紀已存在；非洲也有類似樂器存在數百年，常用於: Simple membranophones sounded by the human voice have existed at least since the sixteenth century; similar instruments have existed in Africa for centuries and are often used in ritual. The claim that Alabama Vest invented it around 1840 has no documentary support. In 1879 Simon Sellers took out a patent for a “toy trumpet” on the same principle. In 1883 Frost patented the “kazoo”, the earliest documented record. In 1902 Smith patented the modern metal kazoo; from 1916 the Original American Kazoo Company made them in Eden, New York, and in 1994 it was the only metal-kazoo maker in North America. In 2010 a kazoo museum opened in Beaufort, South Carolina.
